statement: Maycomb is a small town in the south of the USA.
explanation: It is in Alabama, in the American South.

statement: The play is set in the 1930s.
explanation: It takes place during the Great Depression, a time of great poverty.

statement: Most families in Maycomb have a lot of money.
explanation: It is the time of the Great Depression, and many families are very poor.

statement: In Maycomb, Black people and white people live separate lives.
explanation: Laws and customs kept them apart in schools, churches and many public places.

statement: In the 1930s, Black and white children in Alabama went to the same schools.
explanation: The law said that schools had to be separate.

statement: Children in the South were always expected to say 'ma'am' and 'sir' to adults.
explanation: Good manners were very important in Southern towns.

statement: In a small town like Maycomb, most people are strangers to each other.
explanation: In a small town, almost everyone knows everyone else and their families.

statement: Scout is a girl who says what she thinks.
explanation: She is honest and direct, even when it gets her into trouble.

statement: Atticus often shouts at his children.
explanation: He is calm and patient. He talks to his children and listens to them.

statement: Calpurnia is strict, but she loves the children.
explanation: She keeps them in line because she cares about them.

statement: Boo Radley is a monster, as the children first believe.
explanation: The stories about him are only rumours. He is shy and gentle.

statement: Dill is full of ideas and plans.
explanation: He is the one who keeps wanting to make Boo come out.

statement: Stephanie Crawford keeps other people's secrets.
explanation: She is a gossip. She loves telling everyone's news.

statement: Mayella Ewell has a hard life at home.
explanation: She is poor, lonely and afraid of her cruel father.

statement: Tom Robinson may seem gentle, but he is really a violent man.
explanation: Tom is gentle and kind. He tried to help Mayella.

statement: The Ewells are a very poor family.
explanation: They are one of the poorest families in Maycomb.

statement: Maudie Atkinson is unkind to the Finch children.
explanation: Maudie is a good friend to the children and to Atticus.

statement: Jem does not care what his father thinks of him.
explanation: Jem looks up to Atticus and wants him to be proud.

statement: The play is told by a narrator who remembers her childhood.
explanation: Jean Louise, the grown-up Scout, tells the story and talks to the audience.

statement: In a play, we only learn about a character from what the narrator says.
explanation: We learn about characters from what they say and do, and from what others say about them.

statement: During the Great Depression, many people in the USA lost their jobs.
explanation: It began after the Wall Street Crash of 1929, and millions were out of work.

statement: Farmers in Alabama did well in the 1930s because cotton sold for high prices.
explanation: Cotton prices fell badly, and many farmers were deep in debt.

statement: During the Depression, everyone paid for things with money.
explanation: Many poor families had no cash, so they paid with food, wood or work.

statement: Jim Crow laws kept Black and white people apart in the South.
explanation: They separated people in schools, on buses, in restaurants and in many other places.

statement: In 1930s Alabama, a Black man's word in court counted as much as a white man's.
explanation: All-white juries almost always believed a white person over a Black person.

statement: In a 1930s Southern town, a family's name mattered a lot.
explanation: People were often judged by which family they came from.

statement: In the 1930s, many Southern women worked as lawyers and judges.
explanation: Women had few careers, and in Alabama they could not even sit on a jury.

statement: Atticus treats people with respect, whatever their colour or class.
explanation: He is polite to everyone, from the Ewells to Tom Robinson.

statement: Mrs Dubose has an easy, comfortable life.
explanation: She is old, ill and fighting a painful addiction to morphine.

statement: Scout loses her temper quickly.
explanation: She is ready to fight when someone insults her family.

statement: Dill is happy and settled at home.
explanation: He runs away from home, and he seems to feel unwanted there.

statement: Bob Ewell knows that the people of Maycomb look down on him.
explanation: The town sees his family as the lowest of the low, and he feels it.

statement: Mr Cunningham is a cruel man with no feelings.
explanation: He is a proud father, and Scout's words about his son reach him.

statement: Tom Robinson is polite and careful when he speaks to white people.
explanation: He knows that one wrong word could put him in danger.

statement: Heck Tate is a stranger who knows little about the people of Maycomb.
explanation: As sheriff, he knows the town's families and what they are like.

statement: Boo Radley wants to frighten the children.
explanation: He watches over them kindly and leaves them small gifts.

statement: Mayella Ewell is afraid of her father.
explanation: Bob Ewell is violent, and the evidence suggests he beat her.

statement: Maudie Atkinson is a loyal friend to Atticus.
explanation: She stands up for him when much of the town is against him.

statement: How other characters talk about someone tells us about that person.
explanation: What Maudie and Stephanie say about Boo tells us about Boo, and about them too.

statement: A character's words tell us exactly what they feel.
explanation: People hide their feelings. Actions and small details can show what words hide.

statement: Only Black families were poor in the South during the Depression.
explanation: Many white farmers, like the Cunninghams and the Ewells, were desperately poor too.

statement: Poor white families like the Ewells were treated as equals by Maycomb's 'old families'.
explanation: Maycomb had a strict social ladder, and the Ewells were near the bottom of it.

statement: Some poor white people clung to the idea that they were better than Black people.
explanation: For people with nothing else, being white could feel like the only status they had.

statement: In the 1930s, mobs sometimes took the law into their own hands against Black men accused of crimes.
explanation: Lynchings happened across the South, and the killers were rarely punished.

statement: Black people in 1930s Alabama could vote as freely as white people.
explanation: Poll taxes, unfair tests and threats stopped most Black people from voting.

statement: Children in 1930s Maycomb were usually kept indoors and closely watched.
explanation: Children in small Southern towns had a lot of freedom to play outside.

statement: Atticus believes you must see things from another person's point of view to understand them.
explanation: He teaches his children to imagine standing in someone else's shoes.

statement: Atticus hates Bob Ewell and wants revenge on him.
explanation: Atticus stays calm and controlled, even when Bob Ewell spits in his face.

statement: Mr Cunningham is a decent man who does something terrible when he joins a mob.
explanation: Good people can behave badly in a crowd; Scout reminds him who he really is.

statement: Mayella has plenty of people she can turn to for help.
explanation: She is isolated: white people look down on her family, and she is kept apart from Black people.

statement: Mayella's accusation can be seen as a way of hiding her own shame and fear.
explanation: She broke one of the town's strictest rules and was terrified of her father and of Maycomb.

statement: Tom Robinson's pity for Mayella seemed perfectly acceptable to the white jury.
explanation: For a Black man to feel sorry for a white woman broke the town's racial 'rules'.

statement: Jem's strong sense of fairness makes the injustice around him painful.
explanation: He expects the world to be fair, so he is deeply hurt when it is not.

statement: Stephanie Crawford's gossip is harmless because no one believes it.
explanation: Her stories shape how the children and the town see Boo.

statement: Calpurnia moves between the Black and white communities of Maycomb.
explanation: She works in a white family's home but belongs to the Black community.

statement: Even with a narrator, characters in a play are developed mainly through dialogue and action.
explanation: We judge characters mostly by what they say and do on stage.

statement: Stage directions are spoken aloud to the audience.
explanation: They are instructions for the actors and director about movement, tone and setting.

statement: A character's way of speaking reveals their age, background and education.
explanation: Atticus's careful English and Bob Ewell's rough speech tell us a lot about each man.

statement: An empathic response should be written as a literary essay about the character.
explanation: It is written in the character's own voice, as if you are them.

statement: An empathic response is always written in the first person, as the character.
explanation: You use 'I' and show the character's thoughts and feelings at one moment in the play.

statement: In the 1930s South, Black people could easily find well-paid work in offices and shops.
explanation: Segregation shut them out of most jobs, so many worked as maids, cooks or farm labourers.

statement: Alabama's segregation laws had already ended by the time of the play.
explanation: Jim Crow laws lasted until the civil rights laws of the 1960s.

statement: Ideas of honour and respectability strongly shaped how Southern families behaved.
explanation: Families worked hard to protect their name, and public shame was deeply feared.

statement: A white woman's accusation against a Black man could put his life in danger, whatever the evidence.
explanation: In the Jim Crow South, such accusations often led to a lynch mob or a guilty verdict.

statement: Most people in 1930s Maycomb would have seen Atticus's serious defence of Tom as normal.
explanation: Many people resented him for defending a Black man properly.

statement: Church played only a small part in life in a 1930s Southern town.
explanation: Churches were at the centre of community life for both Black and white people.

statement: Bob Ewell's cruelty can be explained by poverty alone.
explanation: The Cunninghams are just as poor but honest: poverty helps explain his anger, not his choices.

statement: Understanding why Bob Ewell acts as he does is never the same as excusing him.
explanation: Empathy means seeing why someone acts as they do, while still judging what they do.

statement: Mrs Dubose's sharp tongue can be read as a mask for pain and pride.
explanation: She fights her addiction in private; her rudeness hides suffering she will not show.

statement: Atticus thinks Mrs Dubose is simply a bad person.
explanation: He sees her bravery and wants Jem to understand it.

statement: Boo Radley's shyness makes the outside world frightening for him.
explanation: He stays hidden, but he watches the children with care.

statement: Nathan Radley is eager to share his family's private life with the neighbours.
explanation: He keeps his family and its house closed off from the town.

statement: Helen Robinson's situation shows how one verdict can wreck a whole family.
explanation: She loses her husband, and with him her family's income and security.

statement: Reverend Sykes has little influence in his community.
explanation: As pastor, he is a respected leader of Maycomb's Black community.

statement: Scout's temper and honesty come from a strong sense of right and wrong.
explanation: She fights and speaks out because she cannot bear unfairness to her family.

statement: Writers often use a foil, a character who contrasts with another, to make qualities clearer.
explanation: Maudie's kindness and good sense stand out next to Stephanie's love of gossip.

statement: Bob Ewell and Atticus are written as very similar fathers.
explanation: They are foils: one is violent and selfish, the other calm and protective.

statement: Showing what a character does is often more powerful than telling the audience what they are like.
explanation: Writers 'show, not tell', so we work out a character from their actions.

statement: In an empathic response, a character can know what happens later in the play.
explanation: Write only what the character knows and feels at that exact moment.

statement: A good empathic response uses words and expressions the character would really use.
explanation: A character's vocabulary, rhythm and dialect make their voice believable.

statement: The trial in the story is often compared to the real Scottsboro case of the 1930s.
explanation: In 1931 nine young Black men in Alabama were falsely accused and repeatedly convicted by all-white juries.

statement: Harper Lee wrote the story during the 1930s, as such events were happening.
explanation: She published the novel in 1960, looking back on her childhood from the civil rights era.

statement: The novel appeared at a time when the civil rights movement was challenging segregation.
explanation: It came out in 1960, between the Montgomery bus boycott and the Civil Rights Act.

statement: Racism in 1930s Maycomb was mainly the work of a few individuals rather than the system.
explanation: Laws, courts, schools and customs all upheld segregation: it was built into the system.

statement: In the social hierarchy of 1930s Maycomb, class and race together decided a person's place.
explanation: Old white families sat at the top, poor whites below them, and Black people were denied equal rights altogether.

statement: Many white Southerners of the time saw themselves as decent people while upholding an unjust system.
explanation: Prejudice was so normal that many never questioned it, which is what makes the characters believable.

statement: Mayella is written purely as a villain, with no claim on our sympathy.
explanation: She is also a victim of poverty, abuse and loneliness; the play lets us pity her and condemn her at once.

statement: Bob Ewell's racism can be read as a way of claiming a respect he cannot earn.
explanation: Looking down on others lets a man at the bottom of the ladder feel he is above someone.

statement: The play suggests that real courage is moral rather than physical.
explanation: Atticus calls Mrs Dubose brave for fighting her addiction, not for any act of strength.

statement: Tom Robinson is presented as a character with no thoughts or feelings of his own.
explanation: He is shown as kind, honest and afraid, with good reasons for the choices he makes.

statement: The adult Jean Louise understands people in ways that young Scout could not.
explanation: Hindsight lets the narrator see the fear, pride and pain behind adults' behaviour.

statement: The play suggests that people's circumstances have little effect on how they behave.
explanation: Poverty, fear, pride and the times all shape how the characters act.

statement: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something that a character does not.
explanation: The audience may sense Boo's kindness before the children do.

statement: Retrospective narration means a story is told as it happens, without hindsight.
explanation: It is told looking back, so the narrator can comment on what the past meant.

statement: A static character is one who changes greatly during the story.
explanation: A static character stays the same; a dynamic one, like Scout or Jem, changes as they learn.

statement: Dialect in the play is mainly there to make the characters sound comic.
explanation: It shows region, class and education, and it makes the voices authentic.

statement: The mockingbird can be read as a symbol of innocent people who do no harm.
explanation: Characters such as Tom and Boo are often seen as the play's 'mockingbirds'.

statement: A character usually has to be likeable for an audience to understand them.
explanation: We can understand a character's motives without liking them; that is the point of empathy.

statement: In an empathic response, a character's private thoughts can differ from what they say in public.
explanation: The task lets you show what a character feels but could never say aloud.

statement: An effective empathic response mostly retells the events of the scene in order.
explanation: It focuses on thoughts, feelings and attitudes, not on retelling the plot.
